subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 55-year-old man receiving vancomycin for MRSA bacteremia develops flushing, pruritus, and erythema over the face and upper trunk during the infusion. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and there is no airway compromise.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Slow the infusion rate and administer diphenhydramine

explanation_correct: Vancomycin infusion reaction (formerly red man syndrome) is a non-IgE-mediated histamine release triggered by rapid infusion. It is managed by slowing the infusion and giving an antihistamine; stopping the drug permanently is unnecessary.

explanation_incorrect.B: Permanent discontinuation is unnecessary because the reaction is infusion-rate dependent and not true allergy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Epinephrine is reserved for anaphylaxis with airway compromise or shock.
explanation_incorrect.D: Corticosteroids are not first-line for this acute histamine-release reaction.

educationalObjective: Vancomycin infusion reaction is rate-dependent histamine release treated by slowing the infusion and giving an antihistamine.
